title: pg_stat_statements
summary: pg_stat_statements records normalized statement statistics so PostgreSQL tuning starts from workload evidence instead of anecdotes. It is usually the lowest-risk extension in this catalog because it observes query behavior rather than changing the data model, query semantics, or topology. It supports the decision engine by grounding later recommendations in actual time, calls, rows, I/O, and planning pressure.
why_it_exists: It exists because production PostgreSQL systems need a durable way to rank query pain across repeated traffic. Logs and one-off EXPLAIN output are useful, but they do not tell a team which normalized statements dominate total time or whether an optimization changed the workload mix. pg_stat_statements gives reviewers a shared evidence base for index, schema, application, and topology decisions.
when_core_is_enough: Core logs, manual EXPLAIN, and application traces are enough for local exercises, early prototypes, and systems with no repeated query pressure. If the database has no operational owner who will review the statistics, enabling the extension only creates a dashboard ornament.
workload_fit: Adopt for OLTP, read-heavy, analytics-adjacent, and tenant-local workloads where slow paths must be ranked before recommending indexes, replicas, partitioning, or Citus. It is especially useful when teams argue from isolated incidents instead of representative workload windows.
operational_cost: The operational cost is low but real. The team must manage shared_preload_libraries where required, reset cadence, pg_stat_statements.max, query text visibility, and whether track_io_timing or planning counters are available. Sensitive query text may need policy review.
replication_backup_implications: Statistics are local observation data, not application state. They do not need to be preserved in logical backups, but failover and restore runbooks should recognize that a new primary starts with a different statistics history.
not_yet_triggers: No one owns regular workload review.
The system is still a toy or local-only lab with no repeated query mix.
Query text collection would violate a policy that has not been reviewed.

title: pg_trgm
summary: pg_trgm adds trigram similarity operators and index support for typo-tolerant search, fuzzy matching, and substring-heavy lookup. It complements core full-text search; it should not replace lexical ranking, phrase behavior, or exact equality paths. Its best role is narrow and practical: help users find short text values when spelling, spacing, or partial input is messy.
why_it_exists: Users search names, titles, emails, SKUs, support tickets, and catalog labels in ways that exact btree lookup and stemming-based full-text search do not always satisfy. pg_trgm gives PostgreSQL a built-in way to score and index string similarity without introducing a separate search service for modest fuzzy-search needs.
when_core_is_enough: Core btree equality, prefix search, normalized expression indexes, and full-text search are enough when users need exact lookup, stemming, ranking, snippets, or phrase-aware document search. If the workload is really semantic retrieval, pg_trgm should still wait until lexical behavior is proven.
workload_fit: Adopt for search-heavy support UIs, deduplication workflows, product search refinements, and name matching where LIKE or ILIKE queries are visible in latency and users expect typo tolerance. It fits best on targeted columns with measured query pressure.
operational_cost: GIN or GiST trigram indexes can be large and write-heavy. Teams should scope indexes to valuable columns, test similarity thresholds, monitor write amplification, and avoid indexing every text field just because fuzzy search exists. The review should include representative misspellings, false positives, and explain plans so the index supports a product behavior rather than a vague search improvement.
replication_backup_implications: Trigram indexes replicate and restore as normal relation state, but their size and rebuild cost matter in restore drills. Extension availability must be confirmed before restoring schema objects that depend on trigram operators or operator classes.
not_yet_triggers: Core FTS has not been modeled or measured.
The search fields are not known, so index scope would be speculative.
The product needs semantic retrieval rather than fuzzy lexical matching.

title: PostGIS
summary: PostGIS adds spatial types, operators, indexes, and functions for serious geospatial workloads. It is justified when location predicates are core product behavior: containment, intersection, route coverage, distance, service zones, or nearest-neighbor queries. Core PostgreSQL can store coordinates, but PostGIS supplies the spatial semantics and indexing that make those coordinates operationally honest.
why_it_exists: Spatial systems need more than two numeric columns. They need coordinate reference systems, geometry and geography types, spatial predicates, index-assisted bounding operations, and functions that make distance and topology explicit. PostGIS brings those capabilities into PostgreSQL so transactional state and spatial reasoning can remain close together. That matters when dispatch, pricing, compliance, or availability depends on the same write path as the spatial decision.
when_core_is_enough: Core numeric latitude and longitude columns are enough for display-only maps, rare exports, or simple storage where no user-facing spatial predicate exists. If the application only shows a marker and never asks spatial questions, PostGIS is not yet justified.
workload_fit: Adopt for geo-query-heavy logistics, routing, delivery zones, facility search, fleet operations, mapping products, and compliance boundaries where spatial predicates appear on hot paths. It also fits capstones where dispatch combines time, status, tenant, and spatial filters.
operational_cost: The cost is medium. Teams must understand spatial index behavior, coordinate systems, geometry validity, extension upgrade compatibility, larger backups, and managed-service support. Query review needs spatial EXPLAIN literacy, and data-loading pipelines should validate geometry rather than allowing malformed shapes to become production incidents.
replication_backup_implications: Spatial data follows normal PostgreSQL backup and replication paths, but extension version compatibility matters during restore, major upgrades, and migrations between providers. Restore drills should include PostGIS objects and spatial validation queries.
not_yet_triggers: Coordinates are only display metadata.
No hot path uses within, intersects, nearest, or distance predicates.
The team has not chosen coordinate-system and geometry-validity rules.

title: pgvector
summary: pgvector stores embeddings and supports vector distance search inside PostgreSQL. It belongs after the team has modeled documents, metadata filters, permissions, freshness, and lexical search. Its strongest posture is complementary: semantic retrieval can improve recall, but exact terms and relational filters still decide whether a result is useful, current, and allowed.
why_it_exists: Semantic retrieval, recommendations, clustering, and similarity search need vector distance operations near source data. pgvector lets teams keep embeddings in PostgreSQL alongside tenant filters, document metadata, deletion behavior, and transactional updates instead of moving early to a separate vector service. Keeping those controls together is useful when freshness, authorization, and explainability matter as much as nearest-neighbor speed.
when_core_is_enough: Core full-text search, pg_trgm, relational filters, and materialized views are enough when users need exact terms, names, categories, snippets, or auditable ranking. If the search failure is poor lexical modeling, pgvector should not be the first fix.
workload_fit: Adopt for semantic retrieval when embedding volume, refresh cadence, recall targets, and p95 similarity latency are measured. It fits knowledge platforms and recommendation workflows where vector distance solves misses that lexical search cannot address.
operational_cost: The cost is medium to high. HNSW and IVFFlat indexes consume memory and storage, require recall testing, and can complicate bulk refresh. Teams also need embedding lifecycle, model-version, deletion, and reindexing procedures. A useful rollout includes offline evaluation sets and rollback criteria when recall or latency does not justify the index cost.
replication_backup_implications: Vector tables and indexes are normal PostgreSQL data, but restore time, index rebuild memory, and extension availability must be included in drills. Embedding model versions and regeneration procedures should be documented outside the database.
not_yet_triggers: Core lexical search has not been implemented.
Tenant and permission filters are not part of the retrieval plan.
Embedding refresh, deletion, and model-version ownership are undefined.

title: TimescaleDB
summary: TimescaleDB adds hypertables, chunk management, compression, retention helpers, and time-series ergonomics on top of PostgreSQL. It can be valuable for high-volume metrics and event workloads, but Prompt 41 doctrine requires core partitioning, BRIN, materialized views, and scheduled retention to be considered first. The extension should remove measured operational pain, not serve as a time-series label.
why_it_exists: Time-series systems often need predictable chunk lifecycle, retention automation, compression, recent-window query performance, and rollup workflows. TimescaleDB packages those concerns in a mature extension so teams do not have to build every maintenance pattern by hand once scale justifies it.
when_core_is_enough: Core declarative partitioning, BRIN indexes, materialized views, COPY-friendly ingest, and scheduled SQL are enough for moderate ingest, simple retention, and reporting that does not strain maintenance windows. If partition counts and compression needs are modest, stay core and keep the operating model portable until the pain is visible in maintenance duration, storage growth, or query latency.
workload_fit: Adopt for append-heavy metrics or observability workloads where compression, chunk policy, retention automation, and time-window query ergonomics solve measured pain. It fits best when data is centrally time-keyed and lifecycle rules are stable.
operational_cost: The operational cost is significant. Teams must check managed-service availability, extension versions, backup and restore behavior, major upgrades, compression tradeoffs, and whether operations staff understand hypertables rather than plain partitions. Compression policy, chunk sizing, and background jobs become part of production review rather than hidden extension defaults.
replication_backup_implications: Hypertable metadata, jobs, compressed chunks, and extension versions must be restored consistently. Logical replication support and provider-specific backup behavior need explicit review before the extension enters a production plan.
not_yet_triggers: Core partitioning and BRIN have not been measured.
Retention and compression requirements are vague.
Managed-service support or restore behavior is unknown.

title: postgres_fdw
summary: postgres_fdw exposes remote PostgreSQL tables through local foreign tables. It is a bridge capability for migrations, coexistence, validation reads, and carefully bounded federation. The catalog treats it as both core contrib and an extension because the operational posture matters: remote credentials, latency, pushdown, and ownership boundaries become part of every serious recommendation.
why_it_exists: Systems often need old and new PostgreSQL databases to overlap during cutover, backfill, audit validation, or gradual ownership transfer. postgres_fdw lets SQL read remote data without immediately copying everything, which can reduce migration risk when the access paths are narrow and tested.
when_core_is_enough: Core tables, batch ETL, logical replication, or application-level migration code are enough when data has a clear owner and live remote reads are not required. If the bridge would become a permanent hot path, the design is not yet ready. A local copy or publication can be more honest when the product needs predictable latency and ownership.
workload_fit: Adopt for migration-bridge workloads where query paths are bounded, remote SQL pushdown is verified, and the team has a retirement plan. It is especially relevant for modernization capstones and temporary cross-system validation.
operational_cost: The cost is medium. Remote credentials, network latency, transaction semantics, server definitions, planner estimates, and failure behavior cross a boundary that ordinary local SQL does not expose. Monitoring must separate local database health from remote-source failures so support teams know which owner can act.
replication_backup_implications: Foreign table definitions and server mappings back up locally, but remote data does not. Restore plans must identify both sides of the bridge, recreate extension objects, and prove the restored environment can reach or intentionally replace the remote source.
not_yet_triggers: EXPLAIN VERBOSE has not confirmed remote pushdown.
Remote ownership and credentials are unclear.
The bridge has no retirement or materialization plan.

title: PgBouncer
summary: PgBouncer pools client connections in front of PostgreSQL. It is not a PostgreSQL extension, but it belongs in this catalog because connection pressure is one of the earliest operational limits for OLTP systems. The tool helps prevent application worker count from becoming database backend count, especially in autoscaled services and short-transaction workloads. It should be framed as concurrency control, not as a way to hide inefficient transactions.
why_it_exists: PostgreSQL backends are useful but not free. Many web processes, job workers, and serverless-style runtimes create more sessions than the database should run concurrently. PgBouncer gives the platform a controlled admission and reuse layer before max_connections becomes the scaling plan.
when_core_is_enough: Direct connections and disciplined application pools are enough for small services with bounded worker counts, stable sessions, and no connection churn. If the team has not measured connection pressure, PgBouncer may be premature. First confirm current max_connections, active versus idle sessions, pool sizing, transaction duration, and whether application-side pools are already misconfigured.
workload_fit: Adopt for OLTP and read-heavy systems where connection count, idle sessions, or session churn appear before CPU or storage limits. It fits high-concurrency SaaS and APIs with many short transactions.
operational_cost: The cost is medium. Pool mode affects prepared statements, session settings, temporary tables, advisory locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY, authentication, failover routing, and observability. The application must be compatible with the selected mode, and runbooks should explain how to drain, reload, and redirect pools during maintenance or failover.
replication_backup_implications: PgBouncer has no database backup state, but failover and restore runbooks must update pool targets, credentials, health checks, and DNS or service discovery paths.
not_yet_triggers: Application pool limits are unknown.
The workload depends on session state incompatible with transaction pooling.
Connection count is not the measured bottleneck.

title: Citus
summary: Citus distributes PostgreSQL tables across workers for tenant-local scale-out and selected real-time analytics workloads. It is the clearest example of an extension that should often receive candidate_later or avoid_for_now treatment. The distribution key must be obvious from the workload, and hot queries must include it often enough to preserve locality. Without that locality, the cluster adds coordination work instead of removing bottlenecks.
why_it_exists: Some PostgreSQL workloads outgrow one primary while still benefiting from SQL, relational modeling, and PostgreSQL operational familiarity. Citus provides distributed tables, reference tables, co-located joins, and cluster management patterns for workloads that can be sharded by a stable key.
when_core_is_enough: A single primary, partitioning, read replicas, materialized views, query tuning, and connection pooling are enough until one-node limits are measured and workload locality is clear. If the team cannot name the distribution key from query traces, Citus is not yet appropriate. The engine should prefer candidate_later when growth is plausible but locality evidence is missing.
workload_fit: Adopt for strong tenant-local SaaS or analytics workloads where most reads and writes are scoped by tenant, account, customer, or another stable distribution key. It can also fit rollup-heavy analytics when distributed query tradeoffs are understood.
operational_cost: The cost is high. Backups, rebalancing, shard placement, coordinator and worker health, distributed query plans, major upgrades, and managed-service portability all become materially more complex.
replication_backup_implications: Backup and restore must cover coordinator and workers consistently. Replication architecture is provider-specific, and disaster recovery runbooks need cluster-aware validation rather than single-node assumptions. A restore drill should prove reference tables, distributed tables, shard metadata, and application routing together.
not_yet_triggers: No proven distribution key appears on hot paths.
The workload has not exhausted single-primary and partitioning options.
The team cannot operate cluster backup, restore, and rebalancing.

title: ltree
summary: ltree stores label paths and adds operators for hierarchy search. It is useful when ancestor, descendant, subtree, and path-matching predicates are normal product behavior. It should be evaluated after core adjacency lists, recursive CTEs, and materialized paths because many hierarchies do not need extension semantics to be correct or fast enough. The key distinction is whether path search is central enough to deserve a specialized type.
why_it_exists: Trees such as folders, categories, org units, permissions, and product taxonomies often need path containment and subtree search. ltree gives PostgreSQL native path operators and index support for those queries without forcing every hierarchy traversal through recursive SQL.
when_core_is_enough: Adjacency lists, recursive CTEs, closure tables, or plain materialized paths are enough for shallow trees, infrequent hierarchy reads, or models where each edge carries rich metadata. If paths change constantly, ltree may create update pain. Staying core is also preferable when the team has not chosen stable label rules and move semantics.
workload_fit: Adopt for hierarchy path data with frequent subtree reads, permission scopes, catalog navigation, folder search, or label-path matching. It fits best when path labels are stable and the hierarchy is part of read behavior.
operational_cost: The cost is low to medium. Teams must design label rules, handle subtree moves, choose GiST or GIN indexes, and confirm managed-service availability. The data model should still explain ownership and lifecycle of nodes.
replication_backup_implications: ltree data and indexes replicate normally, but extension availability must be checked in target environments before restore or migration. Path values are ordinary data once the extension exists. Restore validation should include representative ancestor and descendant queries, not just table counts.
not_yet_triggers: Recursive CTEs or adjacency lists have not been tested.
Hierarchy edges need rich metadata better represented as rows.
Path labels or subtree-move semantics are unstable.

title: pg_partman
summary: pg_partman automates partition creation and maintenance for PostgreSQL partitioned tables. It should come after the team has already proven that partitioning is needed. Its value is operational rhythm: creating future partitions, managing retention, and reducing the chance that manual partition maintenance becomes an outage source. It is a maintenance tool for a known partitioning strategy, not the reason to partition.
why_it_exists: Time-based and serial partition sets need future partitions before inserts arrive, retention jobs after data ages out, and predictable maintenance across many child tables. pg_partman packages those tasks so teams do not keep rewriting partition-management SQL by hand.
when_core_is_enough: Core declarative partitioning plus scheduled SQL is enough while partition counts are small, retention is simple, and the team can safely maintain partitions manually. If the table is not ready for partitioning, pg_partman is not yet ready either. Manual scripts are acceptable while they remain reviewed, tested, and low frequency.
workload_fit: Adopt for append-heavy event and time-series tables with recurring partition management, retention policies, and operational risk from missed future partitions. It fits mature phase-9 partitioning workflows.
operational_cost: The cost is medium. Background maintenance, configuration tables, extension upgrades, job scheduling, and partition naming conventions become part of operations. Teams must understand both PostgreSQL partitioning and pg_partman behavior. Monitoring should alert before missing future partitions breaks ingest or retention jobs remove the wrong data.
replication_backup_implications: Partition metadata and pg_partman configuration must be restored consistently before maintenance resumes. Restore drills should prove that jobs, future partitions, and retention behavior still work, including the first insert after recovery and the next scheduled maintenance cycle.
not_yet_triggers: Partitioning itself is premature.
Manual partition maintenance is not yet a real operational burden.
Restore drills do not cover partition-management metadata.

title: unaccent
summary: unaccent normalizes diacritics for text search and comparison workflows. It is small, broadly available, and often useful in multilingual search, but it still deserves an explicit workload reason. Accent folding changes semantics, so the product should decide whether cafe and accented cafe should match in the domain. The decision belongs with search relevance, not with convenience defaults.
why_it_exists: Users often type names, titles, authors, and catalog terms without accents even when stored text includes them. unaccent lets PostgreSQL fold diacritics before full-text parsing or normalization so search behavior matches user expectations. It is particularly useful when the corpus is multilingual but the search box is intentionally forgiving.
when_core_is_enough: Core text search is enough when accent-sensitive matching is correct, the corpus is single-language with predictable spelling, or the application already normalizes search fields deliberately. Do not enable it merely because it is inexpensive.
workload_fit: Adopt for search-heavy document, name, catalog, and support workloads with multilingual or accent-insensitive requirements. It fits the full-text-search phase where generated vectors and configurations make normalization inspectable, and where examples can prove that accent folding improves user-visible recall without damaging precision.
operational_cost: The cost is low. The main burden is documenting language expectations, generated-column dependencies, and whether accent folding applies to all search or only selected fields. Teams should test examples where accent folding would be wrong, such as proper nouns or regulated identifiers.
replication_backup_implications: Dictionary configuration, generated search values, and dependent indexes must exist in restored environments. Extension availability is usually straightforward, but restore validation should include representative accent-insensitive search queries and any generated tsvector columns that depend on unaccent normalization.
not_yet_triggers: The product requires accent-sensitive matching.
No multilingual or accent-insensitive search requirement exists.
Search normalization rules have not been documented.

title: pgcrypto
summary: pgcrypto provides functions such as gen_random_uuid and cryptographic helpers inside PostgreSQL. In this curriculum it is most often the practical path for UUID defaults and public identifiers. It should be recommended narrowly: database-generated UUIDs are routine, while encryption and hashing choices require security review rather than casual SQL convenience. The catalog therefore treats UUID generation and broader cryptography as different decisions.
why_it_exists: Applications often need identifiers that can be generated without a central sequence, exposed safely in URLs, or created by multiple writers. pgcrypto gives PostgreSQL a reliable built-in function for random UUID generation and a set of cryptographic primitives for specialized use.
when_core_is_enough: Identity columns, sequences, natural keys, or application-generated identifiers are enough when values do not cross system boundaries and dense internal joins are more important than opaque public references. Security-sensitive hashing may belong in audited application code instead. The engine should not imply that every table needs UUIDs simply because the function is available.
workload_fit: Adopt for relational-core OLTP and migration workloads that need public identifiers, distributed insert IDs, or database-side UUID defaults. It also fits labs where UUID generation should be portable across exercises.
operational_cost: The cost is low for UUID generation. The cost becomes policy-heavy if teams use cryptographic functions for passwords, encryption, or token handling, because key management and compliance requirements are outside simple schema design. Documentation should separate safe defaults from security architecture decisions.
replication_backup_implications: Generated UUID values are ordinary data, and defaults restore cleanly when the extension is installed first. Restore scripts must create the extension before objects that depend on its functions.
not_yet_triggers: Opaque identifiers are not needed.
Dense sequence keys are better for the internal workload.
The intended cryptographic use has not received security review.
